Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette:
Miguel had been living with the memory for more than four decades by the time he came to treatment, but he could still place himself back in the military vehicle where it happened with unnerving clarity. He was a young man then, far from home, and the event had unfolded fast enough that later he struggled to describe it without his hands tightening on the armrests. What stayed with him most was not a single image but the body sensations that arrived with it: the sudden dizziness, the lightheaded drop in his stomach, and a sharp, specific taste that seemed to return before the rest of the scene did. Even now, when that taste came into his mouth unexpectedly, he felt pulled backward into the same helpless moment. He had learned over the years that talking about it could do the same thing. When others asked him to describe his military experience, he became aware of his throat tightening and of how quickly the memory would rise up, not as a distant story but as something immediate and invasive.

After the war, Miguel built a life that looked steady from the outside. He married, later divorced, and eventually became a special education teacher, a role that suited his patience and his ability to remain composed for children who needed structure. But in the background of that life, he began organizing himself around the possibility of feeling trapped. He made a habit of sitting near exits in restaurants, church gatherings, school meetings, and even faculty lunches, telling himself it was simply practical. Before he could relax in any unfamiliar place, he would identify where he could leave quickly if he had to. In classrooms and hallways at work, he quietly checked his surroundings, noting doors, windows, and who was entering or standing too close. He never called this fear; to him it was preparation. Being near the exit made sense because once he felt too enclosed, the memory of the military event seemed closer, and he was certain he would not feel steady again until he knew how to get out.

Miguel also became wary of situations that stirred strong emotion. He noticed that family discussions, memorial services, and even a student's emotional crisis could leave him feeling exposed in a way he did not like. Rather than risk being overwhelmed, he began stepping back from conversations that might become intense, changing the subject or leaving the room when he felt the emotional temperature rising. At school, he remained warm and dependable with his students, but he kept a careful distance from anything that might flood him with feeling. He understood this as staying in control. He had come to believe that once strong emotion got hold of him, it would be harder to keep the memories contained, and he preferred to keep himself on even ground.

In daily life, his watchfulness was constant. He found himself scanning rooms before sitting down, listening for unexpected or loud sounds, and tensing whenever something clanged in the hallway or a door slammed nearby. A dropped metal chair leg, a sudden shout in the corridor, or even an abrupt burst of noise from the school gym could make his body go taut before he had time to think. He remained on guard in ways that others around him did not always notice, though his colleagues sometimes saw him pause and look around before entering a crowded room. Miguel was aware that this left him tired, but he also felt that being superalert was necessary. The world, in his mind, remained unpredictable, and he trusted his own vigilance more than reassurance from anyone else.

By the time he sought help, the symptoms had become harder to ignore because they had begun affecting ordinary parts of his routine. He was still working, still showing up for his students, but the effort of monitoring exits, sounds, and every shift in mood had started to feel exhausting. He was also increasingly aware that the memory was not staying where he wanted it to stay. The taste, the dizziness, and the discomfort of talking about the event had become more intrusive, and he no longer wanted to keep arranging his days around them as though they were simply facts of life. What finally brought him in was not a single crisis but the sense that he was spending too much of his energy bracing for danger. Miguel wanted to understand why a memory from so long ago could still make him feel so alert, so guarded, and so unwilling to sit anywhere unless he knew exactly how to leave. More than anything, he hoped for relief without losing the sense of competence that had carried him through decades of work and family life.
